lines.text: You already make this kind of decision all day. You just don't call it anything.
You get to the front door. If it's raining, you take the umbrella. If it isn't, you leave it on the hook.
That's an if/else. One question that can only be answered yes or no, and two different things that happen depending on which answer you get.
The computer needs it written down more carefully than a person does. Here's that same decision.
The bit in the brackets is the question. It has to be the kind of question with only two possible answers — is it raining works, what's the weather like doesn't.
The line underneath is what happens when the answer's yes. The line after else is what happens when it's no.
One of them runs. Never both. Never neither.
And here's the part that catches people out. The computer doesn't remember having decided. It asks, it does one of the two things, and it moves on.
Next time it comes past, it asks again from scratch.
Which is exactly why an if/else is so useful sitting inside a loop. The question gets asked over and over, and the answer's allowed to come out different every time.
